title: Two-Set Representation Function
content: Defines $r_{A,B}(n)$ as the number of ordered pairs $(a,b) \in A \times B$ with $a + b = n$. This is the central object of the problem. Unlike the single-set representation function $r_A(n) = |\{(a,a') : a+a'=n\}|$ from Problem #28, having two independent sets $A$ and $B$ introduces asymmetry that requires the ratio condition $a_n/b_n \to 1$.
mathContext: $r_{A,B}(n) = \#\{(a,b) \in A \times B : a + b = n\} = \text{Set.ncard}\{p : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \mid p.1 \in A \wedge p.2 \in B \wedge p.1 + p.2 = n\}$

title: Sumset Definition
content: Defines $A + B = \{a + b : a \in A, b \in B\}$ as a set comprehension. In Mathlib the `Pointwise` scoped notation provides `A + B` on sets, but this explicit definition makes the structure clearer for the formalization and avoids potential coercion issues between `Set ℕ` and `Finset ℕ`.
mathContext: $A + B = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : \exists a \in A, b \in B,\; n = a + b\}$

title: Two-Set Basis and Complement Formulation
content: Two equivalent definitions of an asymptotic additive basis: (1) there exists $N_0$ such that every $n \geq N_0$ lies in $A+B$, and (2) the complement $(A+B)^c$ is finite. The equivalence of these formulations is the first theorem proved in Part III. Definition (2) is often more natural in formal proofs because finiteness is a well-developed concept in Mathlib.
mathContext: $\text{IsTwoSetBasis}(A,B) :\Leftrightarrow \exists N_0,\; \forall n \geq N_0,\; n \in A+B \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad (A+B)^c \text{ is finite}$

title: Counting Function
content: The counting function $A(N) = |A \cap [1,N]|$ measures the density of $A$ up to $N$. Implemented by filtering `Finset.Icc 1 N` against membership in $A$. This is the standard way to express growth rates of integer sets; the ratio $A(N)/B(N) \to 1$ is the formalization of $a_n/b_n \to 1$.
mathContext: $A(N) = |A \cap \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}| = |\{a \in A : 1 \leq a \leq N\}|$

title: Asymptotic Ratio Condition
content: The condition $a_n/b_n \to 1$ is expressed via counting functions: $A(N)/B(N) \to 1$ as $N \to \infty$. This uses Mathlib's `Tendsto` and the `atTop` filter. The alternative sequence formulation `HasAsymptoticRatioSeq` states the condition directly on enumerating sequences. This ratio condition is the key hypothesis distinguishing Problem #1145 from its false generalization — Ruzsa's counterexample shows it is necessary.
mathContext: $\text{HasAsymptoticRatio}(A,B) :\Leftrightarrow \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{A(N)}{B(N)} = 1$ via $\text{Tendsto}\;(N \mapsto A(N)/B(N))\;\text{atTop}\;(\text{nhds}\;1)$

title: Basis Equivalence Proof
content: Proves `IsTwoSetBasis A B ↔ IsTwoSetBasis' A B`. Forward direction: if all $n \geq N_0$ are covered, the complement is a subset of $\{0, \ldots, N_0-1\}$, hence finite. Reverse direction: if the complement is finite, take $N_0 = \sup(A+B)^c + 1$. The empty-complement case is handled separately. This is a clean example of `Set.Finite.bddAbove` and `csSup` reasoning in Lean.
mathContext: Forward: $(A+B)^c \subseteq [0, N_0) \Rightarrow (A+B)^c$ finite. Reverse: $N_0 = \sup (A+B)^c + 1 \Rightarrow \forall n \geq N_0,\; n \in A+B$.

title: Finiteness of Representation Pairs
content: Proves that the set of pairs $(a,b)$ with $a + b = n$ is always finite, by embedding it into $[0,n] \times [0,n]$. This is a prerequisite for `Set.ncard` to give meaningful values — without finiteness, `ncard` returns 0 by convention. Uses `Set.Finite.subset` and the product of finite sets.
mathContext: $\{(a,b) : a \in A,\, b \in B,\, a+b=n\} \subseteq [0,n] \times [0,n]$, which is finite.

title: Positive Representation for Sumset Members
content: If $n \in A + B$, then $r_{A,B}(n) \geq 1$: extract a witness pair $(a,b)$ from the sumset membership, show the representation set is nonempty, and apply `Set.ncard_pos`. The proof combines the existential witness with the finiteness lemma above — a pattern that recurs throughout the file.
mathContext: $n \in A + B \Rightarrow \exists (a,b),\; a \in A \wedge b \in B \wedge a+b=n \Rightarrow r_{A,B}(n) \geq 1$

title: Monotonicity of Representation Function
content: If $A \subseteq A'$ and $B \subseteq B'$, then $r_{A,B}(n) \leq r_{A',B'}(n)$. Proved via `Set.ncard_le_ncard` applied to the subset inclusion on representation pairs. This monotonicity is essential for comparing representation functions of different sets — for instance, when restricting to finite subsets of infinite sets.
mathContext: $A \subseteq A',\; B \subseteq B' \Rightarrow r_{A,B}(n) \leq r_{A',B'}(n)$

title: Vanishing for Small Arguments
content: When $n < \min(A) + \min(B)$, no pair $(a,b) \in A \times B$ can sum to $n$, so $r_{A,B}(n) = 0$. The proof shows the representation set is empty by contradiction: any pair would satisfy $a \geq a_0$ and $b \geq b_0$, forcing $a + b \geq a_0 + b_0 > n$. Uses `omega` to close the arithmetic gap.
mathContext: $n < a_0 + b_0$ with $a_0 \leq \min A,\; b_0 \leq \min B \Rightarrow r_{A,B}(n) = 0$

title: The Erdős–Sárközy Conjecture (OPEN)
content: The main conjecture, stated as an axiom since it is an open problem. Under three hypotheses — $A$ and $B$ infinite, $a_n/b_n \to 1$, and $A+B$ is a basis — the conclusion is that $r_{A,B}(n)$ is unbounded: $\forall k,\; \exists n,\; r_{A,B}(n) > k$. This is equivalent to $\limsup r_{A,B}(n) = \infty$. The conjecture carries an implicit \$500 Erdős bounty if it implies the Erdős–Turán conjecture (which it does, as proved below).
mathContext: Axiom: $A^\infty \wedge B^\infty \wedge \frac{a_n}{b_n} \to 1 \wedge \text{IsTwoSetBasis}(A,B) \Rightarrow \forall k,\; \exists n,\; r_{A,B}(n) > k$

title: Self-Representation Reduction
content: When $A = B$, the two-set representation function specializes to the single-set version: $r_{A,A}(n) = |\{(a,a') \in A \times A : a + a' = n\}|$. This is definitional (`rfl`) — no proof obligations. This reduction is the bridge connecting Problem #1145 to Problem #28.
mathContext: $r_{A,A}(n) = |\{(a,a') \in A^2 : a + a' = n\}|$ by definition

title: Self-Ratio is Trivially 1
content: Proves that `HasAsymptoticRatio A A` holds for any infinite set $A$. The ratio $A(N)/A(N) = 1$ for all sufficiently large $N$ (where $A(N) > 0$). The proof constructs an element $a \in A$ with $a > 0$ (from infinitude), then uses `Filter.Ici_mem_atTop` to work eventually, and `div_self` for the arithmetic identity. The `=ᶠ[atTop]` approach elegantly avoids pointwise case splits.
mathContext: $A(N)/A(N) = 1$ for $N \geq \min A$, so $\lim_{N \to \infty} A(N)/A(N) = 1$

title: Problem #1145 Implies Problem #28
content: The key corollary: setting $A = B$ in the Erdős–Sárközy conjecture recovers the Erdős–Turán conjecture. The proof is a one-line application of the main axiom, supplying $A$ for both sets and using `hasAsymptoticRatio_self` to discharge the ratio hypothesis. This makes Problem #1145 strictly stronger than Problem #28 — resolving #1145 would simultaneously settle the \$500 Erdős–Turán bounty.
mathContext: $\text{erdos\_1145\_implies\_28}(A) = \text{erdos\_sarkozy\_conjecture}(A, A, \ldots, \text{hasAsymptoticRatio\_self}(A), \ldots)$

title: Ruzsa's Binary Digit Construction
content: Ruzsa's elegant construction: partition binary digits by position parity. $A$ (ruzsaA) contains numbers whose binary representation has nonzero digits only in even positions ($2^0, 2^2, 2^4, \ldots$), and $B$ (ruzsaB) uses only odd positions ($2^1, 2^3, 2^5, \ldots$). Since every natural number has a unique binary expansion, the interleaving ensures $A + B = \mathbb{N}$ with every representation unique.
mathContext: $A = \{n : \forall k,\; \lfloor n/2^{2k+1}\rfloor \bmod 2 = 0\}$, $B = \{n : \forall k,\; \lfloor n/2^{2k}\rfloor \bmod 2 = 0\}$

title: Ruzsa Counterexample Properties (Axiomatized)
content: Six axiomatized properties of Ruzsa's construction from Problem #331: (1) $A$ is infinite (contains all powers of 4), (2) $B$ is infinite (contains all $2 \cdot 4^k$), (3) unique representations for all $n \geq 1$, (4) bounded representation $r_{A,B} = 1$, (5) $A + B$ is a basis, (6) $a_n/b_n \to 1/2 \neq 1$. These are stated as axioms because their proofs require detailed binary arithmetic that would distract from the main formalization.
mathContext: Ruzsa: $r_{A,B}(n) = 1$ for all $n \geq 1$; $A + B \supseteq \mathbb{N}^+$; $a_n/b_n \to 1/2$

title: Necessity of the Ratio Condition
content: The central negative result: demonstrates that the ratio condition $a_n/b_n \to 1$ is necessary by exhibiting Ruzsa's counterexample. The proof assembles the six axiomatized properties into an existential witness. The $n = 0$ edge case requires a separate argument showing $r_{A,B}(0) \leq 1$ by bounding the pairs set to at most $\{(0,0)\}$. This theorem is the formal justification for why Problem #1145 requires the ratio condition.
mathContext: $\exists A, B : A^\infty \wedge B^\infty \wedge \text{IsTwoSetBasis}(A,B) \wedge \neg(a_n/b_n \to 1) \wedge \exists C,\; \forall n,\; r_{A,B}(n) \leq C$

title: Average Representation Growth
content: Two axiomatized results about averages: (1) a counting identity $\sum_{n \leq N} r_{A,B}(n) \geq A(N) \cdot B(N) - \text{error}$, relating the total representations to the product of counting functions; (2) when both sets have density $\gg \sqrt{N}$, the average representation $\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n \leq N} r_{A,B}(n) \to \infty$. The average-grows result supports (but does not prove) the conjecture: unbounded average implies some values are large, but not necessarily $\limsup = \infty$ pointwise.
mathContext: $\sum_{n=0}^{N} r_{A,B}(n) \geq A(N) \cdot B(N) - \text{error}$; if $A(N), B(N) \gg \sqrt{N}$ then $\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_{n=0}^{N} r_{A,B}(n) \to \infty$

title: Grekos et al. Partial Result
content: An axiomatized partial result extending work of Grekos, Haddad, Helou, and Pihko: under the full hypotheses of Problem #1145, $r_{A,B}(n) \geq 6$ for infinitely many $n$. This is the strongest known unconditional bound toward the conjecture. The original Grekos et al. result was for the $A = A$ case; the extension to two sets uses the ratio condition to transfer the argument.
mathContext: Under the hypotheses of #1145: $\forall M,\; \exists n > M,\; r_{A,B}(n) \geq 6$

title: Commutativity via Pair-Swap Bijection
content: Proves $r_{A,B}(n) = r_{B,A}(n)$ by constructing an explicit bijection $(a,b) \mapsto (b,a)$ between the representation sets. The proof rewrites one set as the image of the other under the swap map, then applies `Set.ncard_image_of_injective`. The injectivity of the swap map on pairs is shown by decomposing the equality of products. This symmetry means the conjecture is invariant under swapping $A$ and $B$.
mathContext: $r_{A,B}(n) = r_{B,A}(n)$ via $(a,b) \mapsto (b,a)$, injective on $\mathbb{N}^2$

title: Vanishing for Large Arguments
content: The complementary bound to `twoSetRepFunc_zero_small`: if $A, B \subseteq [0,N]$, then $r_{A,B}(n) = 0$ for $n > 2N$. No pair $(a,b)$ with $a \leq N$ and $b \leq N$ can sum to more than $2N$. Combined with the small-$n$ vanishing, this brackets the support of $r_{A,B}$ to $[\min A + \min B,\; 2N]$ for finite sets.
mathContext: $A, B \subseteq [0,N],\; n > 2N \Rightarrow r_{A,B}(n) = 0$
